newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Life sentence in Russia often worse than death.
newsitem.headline: Life sentence in Russia often worse than death.

text.p: Russia has suspended executions in line with a promise to the Council of Europe, but a judiciary official said on Thursday that many prisoners pleaded for death after being banished to special camps.
Anatoly Pristavkin, the head of President Boris Yeltsin's commission on pardons, told Reuters about 20 percent of those pardoned did not want to live on.
"We are receiving letters from prisoners sentenced to life imprisonment who are begging for death," he said by telephone.
Prisoners spared by Yeltsin on the committee's recommendation are sent to camps with especially harsh conditions, often in the frozen north.

"Russia has created concentration camps for those with life imprisonment," said Pristavkin, a writer and human rights activist. "It has not followed the European way, where such prisoners are kept in normal jails together with eveyone else."
"The interior ministry has chosen the GULAG way once again. We need better conditions for them. They may yet become normal people -- about a half of them are under 30."

Josef Stalin created a vast system of camps across Russia, largely in Siberia and the Far East. The GULAG network was cut back after the dictator's death and the population of political prisoners has now vanished.
But camp life remains a harsh, unforgiving affair in Russia.
The weekly Itogi magazine said in December that prisoners in two special camps for life inmates were being confined to tiny cells for 23 hours a day. They were not allowed to work, and most were ill.
"Everyone is ill, more than half of them with tuberculosis," Itogi said, accompanying its article with pictures of shaven-headed prisoners in cramped cages
The pardons commission groups 15 people, including writers, journalists and lawyers, and it reviews all possible pardons, not just those involving death penalty.

The Council of Europe called on Russia last June to scrap the death penalty or face suspension. Russia had agreed to abolish capital punishment as one of the conditions for its entry into the organisation.
Pristavkin said Russia had not executed anybody since last May and 501 people were now on the death row of Russian prisons. The interior ministry puts the number at up to 700.
"We have not given the president any new documents since last spring. Without the commission's consent capital punishment cannot be carried out," he said.
But Pristavkin said 53 death sentences were carried out in the first half of last year and nobody was pardoned. In 1995 five people were pardoned and 86 were executed.
Capital punishment in Russia is carried out by a single shot in the back of the prisoner's head.

"The commission had suggested pardoning many more people, but the president was influenced by public opinion, his aides, parliamentary deputies and often the press," said Pristavkin. "I respect his opinion."

Many Russians support the death penalty, especially for serial murderers and rapists. Yeltsin said last year it was too early to abolish capital punishment in Russia, and that Moscow should not give in to the pressure from the West.
In the most notorious case, Andrei Chikatilo, dubbed the "Rostov Ripper", murdered and mutilated 53 boys and women in a 12-year rampage through three Soviet republics. He was executed in 1994.
